claim: Purkinje neurons exhibit membrane bistability when recorded in vitro or in vivo under anesthesia.
source: Purkinje neurons are central to cerebellar function and show membrane bistability when recorded in vitro or in vivo under anesthesia.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: The existence of bistability in vivo in awake animals is disputed.
source: The existence of bistability in vivo in awake animals is disputed.
evidence: Supported by citations in the Introduction section

claim: Purkinje neurons in unanesthetized larval zebrafish exhibit bistability.
source: Here, by recording intracellularly from Purkinje neurons in unanesthetized larval zebrafish (Danio rerio), we unequivocally demonstrate bistability in these neurons.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from intracellular recordings

claim: Tonic firing was seen in depolarized regimes in Purkinje neurons.
source: Tonic firing was seen in depolarized regimes and bursting at hyperpolarized membrane potentials.
evidence: Supported by experimental recordings shown in figures

claim: Bursting occurs at hyperpolarized membrane potentials in Purkinje neurons.
source: Tonic firing was seen in depolarized regimes and bursting at hyperpolarized membrane potentials.
evidence: Supported by experimental recordings shown in figures

claim: Purkinje neurons can switch from one state to another spontaneously or with current injection.
source: In addition, Purkinje neurons could switch from one state to another spontaneously or with current injection.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6

claim: GABAAR is not required for bursting in Purkinje neurons.
source: While GABAAR or NMDAR were not required for bursting, activation of AMPARs by climbing fibers (CFs) was sufficient to trigger bursts.
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments with Gabazine

claim: NMDAR is not required for bursting in Purkinje neurons.
source: While GABAAR or NMDAR were not required for bursting, activation of AMPARs by climbing fibers (CFs) was sufficient to trigger bursts.
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments with APV

claim: Activation of AMPARs by climbing fibers is sufficient to trigger bursts in Purkinje neurons.
source: While GABAAR or NMDAR were not required for bursting, activation of AMPARs by climbing fibers (CFs) was sufficient to trigger bursts.
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments with CNQX and CF stimulation

claim: Initiation of motor neuron spiking is correlated with increased incidence of CF EPSPs.
source: Further, by recording Purkinje neuron membrane potential intracellularly, and motor neuron spikes extracellularly, we show that initiation of motor neuron spiking is correlated with increased incidence of CF EPSPs and membrane depolarization.
evidence: Supported by simultaneous recordings shown in Figure 8

claim: Initiation of motor neuron spiking is correlated with membrane depolarization in Purkinje neurons.
source: Further, by recording Purkinje neuron membrane potential intracellularly, and motor neuron spikes extracellularly, we show that initiation of motor neuron spiking is correlated with increased incidence of CF EPSPs and membrane depolarization.
evidence: Supported by simultaneous recordings shown in Figure 8

claim: Bistability was observed soon after Purkinje neuron specification.
source: Developmentally, bistability was observed soon after Purkinje neuron specification and persists at least until late larval stages.
evidence: Supported by recordings at 4 dpf shown in Figure 9

claim: Bistability persists at least until late larval stages.
source: Developmentally, bistability was observed soon after Purkinje neuron specification and persists at least until late larval stages.
evidence: Supported by recordings at 19 dpf shown in Figure 9

claim: Mammalian Purkinje neurons exhibit high rates of spontaneous activity in vitro.
source: Cerebellar Purkinje neurons have long fascinated neuroscientists due to their elaborate dendritic arbors (Ramón y Cajal, 1911), and their high rates of spontaneous activity in vitro (Llinás and Sugimori, 1980; Raman and Bean, 1999; Han and Bell, 2003) and in vivo (Armstrong et al., 1979; Kitamura and Häusser, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Mammalian Purkinje neurons exhibit high rates of spontaneous activity in vivo.
source: Cerebellar Purkinje neurons have long fascinated neuroscientists due to their elaborate dendritic arbors (Ramón y Cajal, 1911), and their high rates of spontaneous activity in vitro (Llinás and Sugimori, 1980; Raman and Bean, 1999; Han and Bell, 2003) and in vivo (Armstrong et al., 1979; Kitamura and Häusser, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Purkinje neurons are the sole output neuron of the cerebellar cortex.
source: Being the sole output neuron of the cerebellar cortex, the firing patterns of Purkinje neurons are functionally significant for motor co-ordination and motor learning (Thach, 1968; Medina, 2011; Yang and Lisberger, 2014; Hewitt et al., 2015).
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge

claim: The firing patterns of Purkinje neurons are functionally significant for motor co-ordination and motor learning.
source: Being the sole output neuron of the cerebellar cortex, the firing patterns of Purkinje neurons are functionally significant for motor co-ordination and motor learning (Thach, 1968; Medina, 2011; Yang and Lisberger, 2014; Hewitt et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Mammalian Purkinje neurons exhibit membrane bistability in vitro.
source: In addition, mammalian Purkinje neurons exhibit membrane bistability in vitro (Llinás and Sugimori, 1980; Oldfield et al., 2010) and in vivo under anesthesia (Loewenstein et al., 2005; Schonewille et al., 2006), transitioning between 'up' and 'down' states.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Mammalian Purkinje neurons exhibit membrane bistability in vivo under anesthesia.
source: In addition, mammalian Purkinje neurons exhibit membrane bistability in vitro (Llinás and Sugimori, 1980; Oldfield et al., 2010) and in vivo under anesthesia (Loewenstein et al., 2005; Schonewille et al., 2006), transitioning between 'up' and 'down' states.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Mammalian Purkinje neurons transition between 'up' and 'down' states.
source: In addition, mammalian Purkinje neurons exhibit membrane bistability in vitro (Llinás and Sugimori, 1980; Oldfield et al., 2010) and in vivo under anesthesia (Loewenstein et al., 2005; Schonewille et al., 2006), transitioning between 'up' and 'down' states.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: The existence of bistability in Purkinje neurons of awake animals has been the subject of debate.
source: The existence of bistability in Purkinje neurons of awake animals has been the subject of some debate (Schonewille et al., 2006; Yartsev et al., 2009; Engbers et al., 2013) not least because of the difficulty of obtaining intracellular recordings from Purkinje neurons of awake animals.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: There is difficulty in obtaining intracellular recordings from Purkinje neurons of awake animals.
source: The existence of bistability in Purkinje neurons of awake animals has been the subject of some debate (Schonewille et al., 2006; Yartsev et al., 2009; Engbers et al., 2013) not least because of the difficulty of obtaining intracellular recordings from Purkinje neurons of awake animals.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge

claim: The zebrafish cerebellum has three major parts: the corpus cerebelli, the valvula cerebelli, and the vestibulo lateral lobe.
source: The zebrafish cerebellum has three major parts namely, the corpus cerebelli (CCe), the valvula cerebelli (Va) and the vestibulo lateral lobe which is subdivided into eminentia granularis and lobus caudalis cerebelli (Bae et al., 2009; Hibi and Shimizu, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Only the CCe and Va show the characteristic three layered architecture in zebrafish.
source: Of these only the CCe and Va show the characteristic three layered architecture (Hashimoto and Hibi, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: The structure and circuitry of CCe in zebrafish are similar to that seen in electric fish and in mammals.
source: The structure and circuitry of CCe in zebrafish are similar to that seen in electric fish and in mammals (Meek et al., 2008; Hashimoto and Hibi, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Purkinje neurons in zebrafish receive excitatory inputs from parallel fibers and climbing fibers.
source: As in mammals, Purkinje neurons in zebrafish also receive excitatory inputs from parallel fibers (PFs) and climbing fibers (CFs) and inhibition from stellate cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation and schematic in Figure 1A

claim: Purkinje neurons in zebrafish receive inhibition from stellate cells.
source: As in mammals, Purkinje neurons in zebrafish also receive excitatory inputs from parallel fibers (PFs) and climbing fibers (CFs) and inhibition from stellate cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation and schematic in Figure 1A

claim: Purkinje neurons in zebrafish have large planar dendritic arbors decorated with spines.
source: Purkinje neurons in zebrafish, similar to mammalian Purkinje neurons, also have large planar dendritic arbors decorated with spines (Miyamura and Nakayasu, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: Unlike mammals, zebrafish Purkinje neurons do not project to deeper layers but to efferent cells whose somata are present in the Purkinje cell layer or slightly ventral to it.
source: However, unlike mammals, zebrafish Purkinje neurons do not project to deeper layers but to efferent cells whose somata are present in the Purkinje cell layer or slightly ventral to it (Bae et al., 2009; Takeuchi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Efferent cells in zebrafish are also called eurydendroid cells.
source: These efferent cells, also called the eurydendroid cells, receive short axons from the Purkinje neurons, send long projections outside the cerebellum (Bae et al., 2009; Heap et al., 2013; Takeuchi et al., 2015) and are equivalent to the mammalian deep cerebellar nuclear cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Eurydendroid cells are equivalent to the mammalian deep cerebellar nuclear cells.
source: These efferent cells, also called the eurydendroid cells, receive short axons from the Purkinje neurons, send long projections outside the cerebellum (Bae et al., 2009; Heap et al., 2013; Takeuchi et al., 2015) and are equivalent to the mammalian deep cerebellar nuclear cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Zebrin II is expressed in all Purkinje neurons in zebrafish.
source: Zebrin II (aldolase-c, fructose bis-phosphate, a; aldoca) is expressed in all Purkinje neurons in zebrafish (Miyamura and Nakayasu, 2001; Bae et al., 2009), although it is expressed in only a subset of Purkinje neurons in mammals (Doré et al., 1990; Brochu et al., 1990; Leclerc et al., 1992; Sillitoe et al., 2004) and birds (Pakan et al., 2007; Iwaniuk et al., 2009; Corfield et al., 2015; Vibulyaseck et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Zebrin II is expressed in only a subset of Purkinje neurons in mammals.
source: Zebrin II (aldolase-c, fructose bis-phosphate, a; aldoca) is expressed in all Purkinje neurons in zebrafish (Miyamura and Nakayasu, 2001; Bae et al., 2009), although it is expressed in only a subset of Purkinje neurons in mammals (Doré et al., 1990; Brochu et al., 1990; Leclerc et al., 1992; Sillitoe et al., 2004) and birds (Pakan et al., 2007; Iwaniuk et al., 2009; Corfield et al., 2015; Vibulyaseck et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Zebrin II is expressed in only a subset of Purkinje neurons in birds.
source: Zebrin II (aldolase-c, fructose bis-phosphate, a; aldoca) is expressed in all Purkinje neurons in zebrafish (Miyamura and Nakayasu, 2001; Bae et al., 2009), although it is expressed in only a subset of Purkinje neurons in mammals (Doré et al., 1990; Brochu et al., 1990; Leclerc et al., 1992; Sillitoe et al., 2004) and birds (Pakan et al., 2007; Iwaniuk et al., 2009; Corfield et al., 2015; Vibulyaseck et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: The aldoca promoter is used to fluorescently label Purkinje neurons specifically for whole-cell patch clamp recordings.
source: We use the aldoca promoter to fluorescently label Purkinje neurons specifically so as to target them for whole-cell patch clamp recordings (Tanabe et al., 2010; Takeuchi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations and experimental methods

claim: Cerebellar cells start to differentiate at three days post fertilization in zebrafish.
source: In zebrafish, cerebellar cells start to differentiate at three days post fertilization (dpf) and a simple layered structure forms by 5 dpf (Bae et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: A simple layered structure forms by 5 dpf in zebrafish cerebellum.
source: In zebrafish, cerebellar cells start to differentiate at three days post fertilization (dpf) and a simple layered structure forms by 5 dpf (Bae et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: Purkinje neurons appear at 2.8 dpf in zebrafish.
source: Purkinje neurons appear at 2.8 dpf and their numbers stabilize at around 300 neurons by 5 dpf (Bae et al., 2009; Hamling et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Purkinje neuron numbers stabilize at around 300 neurons by 5 dpf in zebrafish.
source: Purkinje neurons appear at 2.8 dpf and their numbers stabilize at around 300 neurons by 5 dpf (Bae et al., 2009; Hamling et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: PF and CF inputs to Purkinje neurons are already present by 5 dpf in zebrafish.
source: By this stage, PF and CF inputs to Purkinje neurons are already present (Bae et al., 2009; Takeuchi et al., 2015; Hamling et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Purkinje neurons are electrically active at 6–7 dpf in zebrafish.
source: Previous studies using calcium imaging and extracellular recording have shown that Purkinje neurons are electrically active at 6–7 dpf (Ahrens et al., 2012; Hsieh et al., 2014; Matsui et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Zebrafish Purkinje neurons exhibit membrane bistability in vivo.
source: Here, we undertake a thorough characterization of spontaneous activity patterns in Purkinje neurons of larval zebrafish. We show that zebrafish Purkinje neurons exhibit membrane bistability in vivo and that the state changes are dependent on AMPAR-mediated CF inputs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript

claim: State changes in zebrafish Purkinje neurons are dependent on AMPAR-mediated CF inputs.
source: Here, we undertake a thorough characterization of spontaneous activity patterns in Purkinje neurons of larval zebrafish. We show that zebrafish Purkinje neurons exhibit membrane bistability in vivo and that the state changes are dependent on AMPAR-mediated CF inputs.
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figures 6 and 7

claim: Loose patch recordings from larval zebrafish Purkinje neurons revealed either tonically spiking or bursting activity.
source: Loose patch recordings from larval zebrafish Purkinje neurons revealed either tonically spiking (Figure 2A, top trace) or bursting (Figure 2A, bottom trace) activity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Two types of events differing in amplitude and waveform were observed in all recorded Purkinje neurons.
source: We also observed two types of events in all the cells we recorded from and these differed in amplitude and waveform (Figure 2B; N = 6 cells).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: The large amplitude events had two distinct phases typical of CF mediated responses.
source: The large amplitude events had two distinct phases typical of CF mediated responses that have been extracellularly recorded in mormyrid fish (Alviña and Sawtell, 2014) and in zebrafish (Hsieh et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by comparison with prior literature

claim: All recorded Purkinje neurons had input resistances above 800 MΩ.
source: All cells had input resistances of above 800 MΩ (2.8 ± 0.75 GΩ, N = 13 cells) and capacitance ranging from 5.6 to 18 pF (13 ± 2.1 pF).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements

claim: Resting membrane potential of Purkinje neurons varied from −40.5 mV to −60.2 mV.
source: Resting membrane potential varied from −40.5 mV to −60.2 mV (−50.3 ± 2.1 mV).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements

claim: 6 out of 13 cells showed bursts of activity punctuated by large amplitude events.
source: 6 out of 13 cells showed bursts of activity punctuated by large amplitude events (Figure 2C, blue arrowheads), while the rest showed tonic spiking interspersed with broad spikes and large amplitude events (Figure 2C,D, green and blue arrowheads respectively).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C,D

claim: Spikes were of larger amplitude and occurred at higher frequencies during bursts than in the tonic mode.
source: Spikes were of larger amplitude and occurred at higher frequencies during bursts than in the tonic mode (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data in Table 1

claim: Narrow attenuated spikes, broad spikes and large amplitude events had distinct peak amplitudes and kinetics.
source: Narrow attenuated spikes, broad spikes and large amplitude events had distinct peak amplitudes and kinetics (Figure 2E and Table 1; Source data in Table 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data in Table 1 and Figure 2E

claim: The narrow spikes are sodium-dependent action potentials.
source: By comparison with in vitro recordings of Purkinje neurons in the central lobe of mormyrid fish (Han and Bell, 2003; de Ruiter et al., 2006), we concluded that the narrow spikes were sodium-dependent action potentials, broad spikes were calcium-mediated spikes and the large amplitude events were CF EPSPs.
evidence: Supported by comparison with prior literature and confirmed by TTX experiments

claim: Broad spikes are calcium-mediated spikes.
source: By comparison with in vitro recordings of Purkinje neurons in the central lobe of mormyrid fish (Han and Bell, 2003; de Ruiter et al., 2006), we concluded that the narrow spikes were sodium-dependent action potentials, broad spikes were calcium-mediated spikes and the large amplitude events were CF EPSPs.
evidence: Supported by comparison with prior literature and confirmed by cadmium experiments

claim: The large amplitude events are CF EPSPs.
source: By comparison with in vitro recordings of Purkinje neurons in the central lobe of mormyrid fish (Han and Bell, 2003; de Ruiter et al., 2006), we concluded that the narrow spikes were sodium-dependent action potentials, broad spikes were calcium-mediated spikes and the large amplitude events were CF EPSPs.
evidence: Supported by comparison with prior literature and confirmed by CNQX experiments

claim: TTX abolishes all types of spontaneous activity in Purkinje neurons.
source: To test whether narrow spikes are sodium action potentials, we bath applied 1 μM Tetrodotoxin (TTX) and observed that all types of spontaneous activity were abolished (Figure 3A; N = 3 cells).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: QX-314 abolished the ability of cells to fire action potentials even when depolarized.
source: QX-314 abolished the ability of cells to fire action potentials even when depolarized (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: In the presence of QX-314, narrow spikes were eliminated while large amplitude events could still be seen.
source: In the presence of QX-314, while narrow spikes were eliminated, large amplitude events could still be seen (Figure 3B, N = 5 cells).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: When network activity was blocked using synaptic receptor antagonists, the large amplitude events were eliminated.
source: In a separate set of experiments, we left sodium channels intact, but blocked network activity using a cocktail of synaptic receptor antagonists. Here, we observed that the large amplitude events were eliminated.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: When network activity was blocked, cells were depolarized and fired tonically.
source: Further, the cells were depolarized (−41.3 ± 0.56 mV) and fired tonically at 38.1 ± 7.4 Hz (Figure 3C; N = 5 cells).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Zebrafish Purkinje neurons fire sodium spikes tonically even when isolated from the network.
source: These experiments demonstrate that the narrow spikes are sodium action potentials and that zebrafish Purkinje neurons fire sodium spikes tonically even when isolated from the network.
evidence: Supported by experimental data with synaptic blockers

claim: Broad spikes could be elicited by strong depolarization, even in the presence of TTX.
source: These broad spikes could be elicited by strong depolarization, even in the presence of TTX (Figure 4B), indicating that these events do not require voltage-gated sodium channels.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Broad spikes do not require voltage-gated sodium channels.
source: These broad spikes could be elicited by strong depolarization, even in the presence of TTX (Figure 4B), indicating that these events do not require voltage-gated sodium channels.
evidence: Inferred from TTX experiments

claim: Broad spikes were abolished after exposure to cadmium chloride.
source: Broad spikes were abolished after exposure to 200 μM Cadmium chloride (Figure 4C), thus indicating that these events are calcium spikes triggered when the cell is depolarized.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Broad spikes are calcium spikes triggered when the cell is depolarized.
source: Broad spikes were abolished after exposure to 200 μM Cadmium chloride (Figure 4C), thus indicating that these events are calcium spikes triggered when the cell is depolarized.
evidence: Inferred from cadmium experiments

claim: The rheobase for broad spikes was consistently higher than that of sodium spikes.
source: The rheobase for the broad spikes (43.1 ± 7.1 pA; N = 8 cells) was consistently higher than that of sodium spikes (8.6 ± 1.2 pA; N = 7 cells; p < 0.001; Mann–Whitney; Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A

claim: The peak amplitude of large amplitude events decreased linearly with increasing depolarization.
source: As will be expected of synaptic events, we observed that the peak amplitude decreased linearly with increasing depolarization (Figure 5A, Pearson's r = −0.8, p < 0.001, N = 5 cells), while the inter-event interval did not change (Figure 5B; Pearson's r = −0.04, p = 0.33).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A

claim: The inter-event interval of large amplitude events did not change with membrane potential.
source: As will be expected of synaptic events, we observed that the peak amplitude decreased linearly with increasing depolarization (Figure 5A, Pearson's r = −0.8, p < 0.001, N = 5 cells), while the inter-event interval did not change (Figure 5B; Pearson's r = −0.04, p = 0.33).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: In the presence of APV, the large amplitude events were not affected.
source: In the presence of the NMDAR blocker APV, the large amplitude events were not affected (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, N = 5 cells).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: CNQX completely abolished the large amplitude events.
source: However, the AMPAR blocker CNQX completely abolished the large amplitude events (Figure 5C; N = 12 cells), thus showing that these are indeed AMPAR-mediated synaptic currents.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: The large amplitude events are AMPAR-mediated synaptic currents.
source: However, the AMPAR blocker CNQX completely abolished the large amplitude events (Figure 5C; N = 12 cells), thus showing that these are indeed AMPAR-mediated synaptic currents.
evidence: Inferred from CNQX experiments

claim: The large amplitude events reversed at around +12 mV.
source: Consistent with this, these events reversed at around +12 mV (Figure 5D), close to AMPAR reversal potential.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D

claim: CF stimulation produced all-or-none EPSCs similar in size to spontaneously occurring large amplitude events.
source: As the stimulus amplitude was gradually increased, large amplitude EPSCs similar in size to the spontaneously occurring large amplitude events were seen (Figure 5E). These were all-or-none in that no EPSCs of intermediate amplitudes were seen.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E

claim: CF EPSCs were all-or-none with no EPSCs of intermediate amplitudes.
source: As the stimulus amplitude was gradually increased, large amplitude EPSCs similar in size to the spontaneously occurring large amplitude events were seen (Figure 5E). These were all-or-none in that no EPSCs of intermediate amplitudes were seen.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E

claim: CNQX abolished the all-or-none CF EPSCs.
source: When CNQX was added to the bath, the all-or-none CF EPSCs were completely abolished, confirming that the large amplitude events are AMPAR mediated all-or-none CF EPSPs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E

claim: The large amplitude events are AMPAR mediated all-or-none CF EPSPs.
source: When CNQX was added to the bath, the all-or-none CF EPSCs were completely abolished, confirming that the large amplitude events are AMPAR mediated all-or-none CF EPSPs.
evidence: Inferred from CF stimulation and CNQX experiments

claim: Small amplitude synaptic currents are putative PF mediated synaptic currents.
source: In addition to the CF EPSCs, we also observed small amplitude synaptic currents (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, panel A, green arrowheads), which were also abolished by CNQX, suggesting that these are putative PF mediated synaptic currents.
evidence: Inferred from CNQX experiments

claim: CF and PF EPSCs were distinct in their amplitudes.
source: CF and PF EPSCs were distinct in their amplitudes, with CF EPSCs consistently crossing 200 pA in peak amplitude while the PF EPSCs were usually smaller than 100 pA (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, panel B; p < 0.0001, Mann–Whitney test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2

claim: PF EPSCs had consistently larger CVs across cells than CF EPSCs.
source: We computed the coeffecient of variation (CV) of peak amplitudes of CF and PF EPSCs and found that the PF EPSCs had consistently larger CVs across cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, panel C; N = 6 cells; p = 0.0087, Mann–Whitney).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2

claim: Blocking synaptic receptors with APV, CNQX and Bicuculline/Gabazine eliminates bursting and causes neurons to show tonic spiking.
source: As mentioned above, blocking synaptic receptors with APV, CNQX and Bicuculline/Gabazine eliminates bursting and causes the neurons to show tonic spiking (Figure 3C; N = 5 cells).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Purkinje neurons could spontaneously toggle between the bursting and tonic states.
source: We also found that Purkinje neurons could spontaneously toggle between the bursting and tonic states (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A

claim: 3 out of 8 tonic cells spontaneously hyperpolarized and entered the bursting state.
source: 3 out of 8 tonic cells spontaneously hyperpolarized during the course of our recording and entered the bursting state.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: 4 out of 11 cells spontaneously depolarized and toggled from the bursting to tonically firing state.
source: Conversely, 4 out of 11 cells spontaneously depolarized and toggled from the bursting to tonically firing state.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: Tonic cells were significantly more depolarized compared to bursting cells.
source: We examined the basal membrane potential in bursting and tonic cells and found that tonic cells were significantly more depolarized (−43.7 ± 1.1 mV, N = 8 cells) compared to bursting cells (−56.3 ± 1.6 mV; N = 11 cells; p < 0.001; Mann–Whitney; Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B

claim: Bursting cells could be made to fire tonically by depolarizing them.
source: In addition, 4 of 4 bursting cells could be made to fire tonically by depolarizing them and 4 of 4 tonic cells could generate bursts when they were hyperpolarized with negative current.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: Tonic cells could generate bursts when hyperpolarized with negative current.
source: In addition, 4 of 4 bursting cells could be made to fire tonically by depolarizing them and 4 of 4 tonic cells could generate bursts when they were hyperpolarized with negative current.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: When synaptic receptors were blocked, tonic cells lost the ability to generate bursts upon hyperpolarization and became silent.
source: When we bath applied CNQX, APV and Bicuculline, tonic cells lost the ability to generate bursts upon hyperpolarization and became silent (N = 5 cells).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: In the presence of APV, Purkinje neurons were still able to generate bursts.
source: In the presence of 40 μM APV (N = 5 cells) Purkinje neurons were still able to generate bursts (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C

claim: In the presence of Gabazine, bursts could still be seen though of altered shape and amplitude.
source: In the presence of 10 μM Gabazine (N = 10 cells), bursts, though of altered shape and amplitude, could still be seen (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D

claim: CNQX completely abolished bursting behavior.
source: However, 20 μM CNQX completely abolished bursting behavior (Figure 6E; N = 12 cells), indicating that AMPAR and not GABAAR or NMDAR were responsible for triggering bursts in the hyperpolarized state.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E

claim: AMPAR and not GABAAR or NMDAR are responsible for triggering bursts in the hyperpolarized state.
source: However, 20 μM CNQX completely abolished bursting behavior (Figure 6E; N = 12 cells), indicating that AMPAR and not GABAAR or NMDAR were responsible for triggering bursts in the hyperpolarized state.
evidence: Inferred from pharmacological experiments

claim: Purkinje neurons have two stable states: tonic spiking in the 'up' state and bursting when toggled from 'down' states.
source: From these experiments, we conclude that Purkinje neurons have two stable states. Tonic spiking occurs in the 'up' state and when the neurons are in the 'down' state, AMPAR-mediated synaptic inputs can toggle the cell to 'up' states thus generating bursts.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations

claim: AMPAR-mediated synaptic inputs can toggle the cell from 'down' to 'up' states thus generating bursts.
source: From these experiments, we conclude that Purkinje neurons have two stable states. Tonic spiking occurs in the 'up' state and when the neurons are in the 'down' state, AMPAR-mediated synaptic inputs can toggle the cell to 'up' states thus generating bursts.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations

claim: Burst initiation was usually marked by the presence of CF-EPSPs.
source: Indeed, we observed that burst initiation was usually marked by the presence of CF-EPSPs (Figure 7A, blue arrowheads).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A

claim: There was a significant increase in the number of CF-EPSPs immediately preceding burst onset.
source: When the burst initiation was calculated from the first sodium spike (Figure 7A, red arrowhead), we observed a significant increase in the number of CF-EPSPs from an average of 32.34 events per 200 ms bin to 92 events in a 200 ms bin immediately preceding the spike (Figure 7B; N = 5 cells; p < 0.001; Chi-square test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B

claim: CF activation triggered bursting in Purkinje neurons without fail.
source: Next, we stimulated CF in the presence of Gabazine and APV and observed that CF activation triggered bursting in Purkinje neurons without fail (Figure 7C; N = 5 cells).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C

claim: Addition of CNQX abolishes the ability of CF stimulation to trigger CF-EPSPs and to trigger bursts.
source: Addition of CNQX abolishes the ability of CF stimulation to trigger CF-EPSPs and to trigger bursts (Figure 7D; N = 5 cells).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D

claim: AMPAR-mediated CF-EPSPs are sufficient to trigger bursting in Purkinje neurons when the neurons are in the hyperpolarized state.
source: These data argue that AMPAR-mediated CF-EPSPs are sufficient to trigger bursting in Purkinje neurons when the neurons are in the hyperpolarized state.
evidence: Inferred from CF stimulation experiments

claim: Motor episode initiation was usually accompanied by the initiation of bursting in the Purkinje neuron.
source: We found that motor episode initiation was usually accompanied by the initiation of bursting in the Purkinje neuron (Figure 8A; N = 5 cells).
evidence: Supported by simultaneous recordings shown in Figure 8A

claim: CF-EPSPs tended to be clustered around the initiation of motor episodes.
source: CF-EPSPs tended to be clustered around the initiation of motor episodes (Figure 8B and 0 on x-axis).
evidence: Supported by raster plot shown in Figure 8B

claim: The number of CF-EPSPs occurring within a 1 s window after motor episode initiation was significantly higher than average.
source: The number of CF-EPSPs occurring within a 1 s window after motor episode initiation (169) was significantly higher than average (40, p < 0.001, Chi-square test; Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by peri-event time histogram shown in Figure 8C

claim: The membrane potential at +0.5 s was significantly higher than that at −0.5 s when motor episodes were aligned at 0 s.
source: The membrane potential at +0.5 s was significantly higher by 17 ± 0.93 mV (N = 107 trials, p < 0.001) than that at −0.5 s, when motor episodes were aligned at 0 s (Figure 8D,E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D,E

claim: Depolarization latency and reliability were variable across the cells recorded from.
source: However, depolarization latency and reliability were variable across the cells we recorded from.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 8E

claim: The initiation of motor episodes is accompanied by an increased incidence of CF-EPSPs in the Purkinje neuron, which toggle it to the 'up' state.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that the initiation of motor episodes is accompanied by an increased incidence of CF-EPSPs in the Purkinje neuron, which toggle it to the 'up' state.
evidence: Inferred from simultaneous recordings of Purkinje neurons and motor episodes

claim: Individual Purkinje neurons exhibit variability in how they represent the time of initiation of motor episodes.
source: However, individual Purkinje neurons exhibit variability in how they represent the time of initiation of motor episodes.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations shown in Figure 8E

claim: At 4 dpf, spontaneous activity was indistinguishable from that seen at 7 dpf.
source: We recorded at 4 dpf, which is the earliest time point when Purkinje neurons can be unequivocally identified. At this stage, the spontaneous activity was indistinguishable from that seen at 7 dpf.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: Both bursting and tonic Purkinje neurons were present at 4 dpf.
source: Both bursting and tonic Purkinje neurons were present (N = 5 cells in tonic mode, 2 cells in bursting mode).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations at 4 dpf

claim: CF-EPSPs, sodium spikes and calcium spikes were present at 4 dpf.
source: CF-EPSPs could be identified, and narrow sodium spikes as well as broad calcium spikes were also present (Figure 9A, top trace).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9A

claim: At 19 dpf, CF-EPSPs, sodium spikes and calcium spikes were present.
source: At 19 dpf, the latest stage we recorded from, again we were able to detect CF-EPSPs, sodium spikes and calcium spikes.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations at 19 dpf

claim: Of 10 cells recorded at 19 dpf, 7 were tonically firing and 3 were bursting.
source: Of 10 cells recorded at 19 dpf, 7 were tonically firing and 3 were bursting (Figure 9A, bottom trace).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations at 19 dpf

claim: At both 4 dpf and 19 dpf, tonic and bursting cells could be mode-switched by hyperpolarization and depolarization respectively.
source: As in 7 dpf larvae, both at 4 dpf and at 19 dpf, tonic and bursting cells could be mode-switched by hyperpolarization and depolarization respectively.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: At 19 dpf, fewer CF-EPSPs were observed as compared to 4 dpf or 7 dpf.
source: However, one key point of difference was that at 19 dpf, we observed fewer CF-EPSPs as compared to 4 dpf or 7 dpf.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: The peak amplitude of CF-EPSCs increased significantly between 7 dpf and 19 dpf.
source: We found that the peak amplitude and inter-event interval of CF-EPSCs increased significantly between 7 dpf and 19 dpf (Figure 9B–D, p < 0.0001, Kruskal–Wallis), thus confirming that as the larva matures, Purkinje neurons receive fewer but stronger CF EPSCs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9B-D

claim: The inter-event interval of CF-EPSCs increased significantly between 7 dpf and 19 dpf.
source: We found that the peak amplitude and inter-event interval of CF-EPSCs increased significantly between 7 dpf and 19 dpf (Figure 9B–D, p < 0.0001, Kruskal–Wallis), thus confirming that as the larva matures, Purkinje neurons receive fewer but stronger CF EPSCs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9B-D

claim: As the larva matures, Purkinje neurons receive fewer but stronger CF EPSCs.
source: We found that the peak amplitude and inter-event interval of CF-EPSCs increased significantly between 7 dpf and 19 dpf (Figure 9B–D, p < 0.0001, Kruskal–Wallis), thus confirming that as the larva matures, Purkinje neurons receive fewer but stronger CF EPSCs.
evidence: Inferred from developmental changes in CF-EPSC properties

claim: The coefficient of variation of CF-EPSC peak amplitude decreased from 0.6 at 4 dpf to 0.4 at 19 dpf.
source: The coefficient of variation of CF-EPSC peak amplitude was 0.6 at 4 dpf, 0.5 at 7 dpf and 0.4 at 19 dpf, suggesting a gradual pruning of CF inputs from 4 dpf to 19 dpf.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: There is a gradual pruning of CF inputs from 4 dpf to 19 dpf.
source: The coefficient of variation of CF-EPSC peak amplitude was 0.6 at 4 dpf, 0.5 at 7 dpf and 0.4 at 19 dpf, suggesting a gradual pruning of CF inputs from 4 dpf to 19 dpf.
evidence: Inferred from changes in coefficient of variation

claim: Purkinje neurons in vivo in the absence of anesthesia exhibit membrane bistability with tonic firing during 'up' states and burst firing during 'down' states.
source: We have shown that Purkinje neurons, in vivo, in the absence of anesthesia exhibit membrane bistability, with tonic firing during 'up' states and burst firing during 'down' states.
evidence: Supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript

claim: Burst firing happens when the membrane is transiently toggled to 'up' states.
source: Burst firing happens when the membrane is transiently toggled to 'up' states and these transitions to 'up' states can be driven by AMPAR mediated excitation.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations

claim: Transitions to 'up' states can be driven by AMPAR mediated excitation.
source: Burst firing happens when the membrane is transiently toggled to 'up' states and these transitions to 'up' states can be driven by AMPAR mediated excitation.
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments

claim: CF inputs are the source for the strong AMPAR excitation required for state transitions.
source: We have shown that CF inputs are the source for the strong AMPAR excitation required for these state transitions.
evidence: Supported by CF stimulation experiments

claim: Purkinje neurons may utilize CF-driven bistability to create a distributed representation of the timing of motor events.
source: Our data suggest that Purkinje neurons may utilize CF-driven bistability to create a distributed representation of the timing of motor events.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of experimental data

claim: The cerebellum is functionally mature at least by 7 dpf in zebrafish.
source: Nevertheless, other factors suggest that the cerebellum is functionally mature at least by 7 dpf and that the bistability observed is integral to this function.
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of evidence

claim: Calcium imaging in 6–7 dpf larvae has revealed Purkinje neurons to be active during optomotor and optokinetic responses.
source: Calcium imaging in 6–7 dpf larvae has revealed Purkinje neurons to be active during optomotor and optokinetic responses (Ahrens et al., 2012; Matsui et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Optogenetic silencing of Purkinje neurons interfered with optomotor and optokinetic responses in larval zebrafish.
source: Optogenetic silencing of Purkinje neurons interfered with optomotor and optokinetic responses in larval zebrafish of this age (Matsui et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: The cerebellum has been shown to be involved in associative learning in adult vertebrates.
source: The cerebellum has been shown to be involved in associative learning in adult vertebrates such as goldfish, rodents, rabbits and non-human primates (Thompson and Steinmetz, 2009; Gómez et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Ablation of the entire CCe in 6–8 dpf zebrafish larvae resulted in deficits in associative learning in a classical conditioning paradigm.
source: Ablation of the entire CCe in 6–8 dpf zebrafish larvae resulted in deficits in associative learning in a classical conditioning paradigm (Aizenberg and Schuman, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: The functioning of the larval cerebellum is analogous to its function in the adult.
source: These studies provide support to the idea that the functioning of the larval cerebellum is analogous to its function in the adult and that the activity patterns we recorded are functionally relevant in the larva and in the adult.
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of evidence from prior literature

claim: The cerebellum is one of the oldest parts of the vertebrate brain and is present in all vertebrates.
source: The cerebellum or 'little brain' is one of the oldest parts of the vertebrate brain and is present in all vertebrates (Bell, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: Among gnathostomes, the circuitry of the cerebellum is remarkably conserved with most major cell types being present in the cerebellums of cartilaginous fish, bony fish, and tetrapods.
source: Among gnathostomes, the circuitry of the cerebellum is remarkably conserved with most major cell types being present in the cerebellums of cartilaginous fish, bony fish, and tetrapods (Nieuwenhuys et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: Zebrafish and mammals diverged from a common ancestor 450 million years ago.
source: Although zebrafish and mammals diverged from a common ancestor 450 million years ago, structurally, the cerebellum of zebrafish shows a high degree of similarity with mammalian cerebellar circuits.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge

claim: The cerebellum of zebrafish shows a high degree of similarity with mammalian cerebellar circuits.
source: Although zebrafish and mammals diverged from a common ancestor 450 million years ago, structurally, the cerebellum of zebrafish shows a high degree of similarity with mammalian cerebellar circuits.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge

claim: In contrast to mammals, zebrafish do not have deep cerebellar nuclei and the efferent cells are placed proximal to Purkinje neurons within the ganglionic layer.
source: In contrast to mammals, zebrafish do not have deep cerebellar nuclei and the efferent cells are placed proximal to Purkinje neurons within the ganglionic layer; CFs make synaptic contacts on the somata and proximal dendrites of Purkinje neurons and do not ramify extensively within the molecular layer; and basket cells have so far not been identified in zebrafish (Bae et al., 2009; Takeuchi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: CFs make synaptic contacts on the somata and proximal dendrites of Purkinje neurons in zebrafish and do not ramify extensively within the molecular layer.
source: In contrast to mammals, zebrafish do not have deep cerebellar nuclei and the efferent cells are placed proximal to Purkinje neurons within the ganglionic layer; CFs make synaptic contacts on the somata and proximal dendrites of Purkinje neurons and do not ramify extensively within the molecular layer; and basket cells have so far not been identified in zebrafish (Bae et al., 2009; Takeuchi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Basket cells have so far not been identified in zebrafish.
source: In contrast to mammals, zebrafish do not have deep cerebellar nuclei and the efferent cells are placed proximal to Purkinje neurons within the ganglionic layer; CFs make synaptic contacts on the somata and proximal dendrites of Purkinje neurons and do not ramify extensively within the molecular layer; and basket cells have so far not been identified in zebrafish (Bae et al., 2009; Takeuchi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: In zebrafish larvae, the rostromedial cerebellum corresponds to spinocerebellum and the caudolateral regions correspond to vestibulocerebellum.
source: In addition, in zebrafish larvae, the rostromedial cerebellum corresponds to spinocerebellum and the caudolateral regions correspond to vestibulocerebellum; the cerebrocerebellar hemispheres are entirely absent (Matsui et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: The cerebrocerebellar hemispheres are entirely absent in zebrafish larvae.
source: In addition, in zebrafish larvae, the rostromedial cerebellum corresponds to spinocerebellum and the caudolateral regions correspond to vestibulocerebellum; the cerebrocerebellar hemispheres are entirely absent (Matsui et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: Unlike mammalian Purkinje neurons, zebrafish larval Purkinje neurons do not exhibit complex spikes.
source: Unlike mammalian Purkinje neurons, zebrafish larval Purkinje neurons do not exhibit complex spikes. Instead, they show large amplitude all-or-none CF EPSPs and broad calcium spikes.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: Zebrafish larval Purkinje neurons show large amplitude all-or-none CF EPSPs and broad calcium spikes.
source: Unlike mammalian Purkinje neurons, zebrafish larval Purkinje neurons do not exhibit complex spikes. Instead, they show large amplitude all-or-none CF EPSPs and broad calcium spikes.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: Spontaneous firing is an intrinsic property of zebrafish Purkinje neurons.
source: Similar to mammalian neurons, spontaneous firing appears to be an intrinsic property of zebrafish Purkinje neurons as these neurons continue to fire at high rates even when fast synaptic transmission is blocked, as has been shown in rodent Purkinje neurons in cerebellar slices (Häusser and Clark, 1997).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and comparison with prior literature

claim: Two kinds of glutamatergic excitation are observed in zebrafish Purkinje neurons: strong excitation from CFs and weak excitation from PFs, both mediated by AMPA receptors.
source: Secondly, like in mammalian Purkinje neurons, two kinds of glutamatergic excitation are observed: strong excitation from CFs and weak excitation from PFs, both mediated by AMPA receptors (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2

claim: Bistability is a conserved feature of Purkinje neurons from fish to mammals.
source: Based on the conservation of other structural and functional properties of the cerebellum, it seems reasonable to conclude that bistability is a conserved feature of Purkinje neurons from fish to mammals.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations and evolutionary considerations

claim: In zebrafish, GABAergic inhibition or NMDAR-dependent excitation seem not to be critical for generating bursts.
source: In zebrafish, GABAergic inhibition or NMDAR-dependent excitation seem not to be critical for generating bursts.
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments

claim: Both a hyperpolarized membrane potential and AMPAR-mediated CF-activation were required for triggering bursts.
source: Both a hyperpolarized membrane potential and AMPAR-mediated CF-activation were required for triggering bursts, suggesting that CF-EPSPs activate voltage-dependent conductances in the Purkinje neuron to trigger bursts.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: CF-EPSPs activate voltage-dependent conductances in the Purkinje neuron to trigger bursts.
source: Both a hyperpolarized membrane potential and AMPAR-mediated CF-activation were required for triggering bursts, suggesting that CF-EPSPs activate voltage-dependent conductances in the Purkinje neuron to trigger bursts.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations

claim: The three elements of spontaneous activity in zebrafish Purkinje neurons (sodium spikes, calcium spikes and CF-EPSPs) are all present within a day after they differentiate.
source: We report here that the three elements of spontaneous activity in zebrafish Purkinje neurons, namely, sodium spikes, calcium spikes and CF-EPSPs are all present within a day after they differentiate (Figure 9).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9

claim: Bistability appears soon after Purkinje neuron specification and persists at least until 19 dpf.
source: Further, bistability also appears soon after Purkinje neuron specification and persists at least until 19 dpf, indicating that Purkinje neuron electrical properties mature rapidly.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations at different developmental stages

claim: Purkinje neuron electrical properties mature rapidly.
source: Further, bistability also appears soon after Purkinje neuron specification and persists at least until 19 dpf, indicating that Purkinje neuron electrical properties mature rapidly.
evidence: Inferred from developmental observations

claim: In adult vertebrates, each Purkinje neuron is innervated by a single CF.
source: In adult vertebrates, each Purkinje neuron is innervated by a single CF.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge

claim: CF to Purkinje neuron synapses progress from polyinnervation to single innervation through a process of synapse elimination.
source: Analogous to the neuromuscular junction, CF to Purkinje neuron synapses progress from polyinnervation to single innervation through a process of synapse elimination.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge

claim: In rodents, the process of CF synapse elimination occurs during the first two weeks of post-natal life.
source: In rodents, this process occurs during the first two weeks of post-natal life (Hashimoto and Kano, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: Purkinje neuron bursts are highly correlated with motor neuronal spikes.
source: We have shown that Purkinje neuron bursts are highly correlated with motor neuronal spikes.
evidence: Supported by simultaneous recordings shown in Figure 8

claim: Initiation of motor episodes is accompanied by increase in CF inputs that depolarize the Purkinje neurons.
source: Our data reveal that initiation of motor episodes is accompanied by increase in CF inputs that depolarize the Purkinje neurons (Figure 8).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8

claim: Depolarization triggers bursts, presumably by recruiting persistent sodium, high threshold calcium and calcium-dependent potassium conductances and/or due to co-incident PF inputs.
source: Such depolarization triggers bursts, presumably by recruiting persistent sodium, high threshold calcium and calcium-dependent potassium conductances and/or due to co-incident PF inputs.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of experimental observations

claim: Mode switching could serve as a 'clutch' that engages or disengages Purkinje neuron activity to locomotor behavior.
source: Though we did not find a tonic cell during our simultaneous motor episode recordings, we propose that mode switching could serve as a 'clutch' that engages or disengages Purkinje neuron activity to locomotor behavior.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of experimental observations

claim: By mode switching from tonic to bursting, Purkinje neurons might choose to 'listen in' on locomotion related neural inputs.
source: By mode switching from tonic to bursting, Purkinje neurons might choose to 'listen in' on locomotion related neural inputs.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of experimental observations

claim: The time to peak depolarization was different for different cells.
source: We also observed heterogeneity in the timing of Purkinje neuron depolarization with respect to motor episode initiation. The time to peak depolarization was different for different cells (Figure 8E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8E

claim: Purkinje neurons might use CF-driven bursting to generate a distributed representation of motor events.
source: This leads us to propose that Purkinje neurons might use CF-driven bursting to generate a distributed representation of motor events.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of experimental observations
